title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
blurb: Tests the two stages of RAG, why sentence embeddings beat TF-IDF on paraphrased queries, cosine similarity and approximate search, chunk size and overlap, the failure modes to plan for, and when RAG or fine-tuning is the right tool.

refLinks.label: §31.2.1 Dense Embeddings vs. What Chapter 27 Covered

ideas.title: Failure modes and the fallback path
A paraphrased query against TF-IDF and embeddings

questions.prompt: Which step happens offline, before any user asks a question?
options: Building a prompt from the retrieved chunks and the user's original query
Splitting documents into chunks and storing their embeddings
Embedding the user's query with the same model
Asking the LLM to answer from the retrieved text
questions.explanation: Indexing (chunk, embed, store) is done once and updated as data changes. Embedding the query, building the augmented prompt and generating all happen online, once per query.

questions.prompt: Why is RAG usually the first choice when a customer wants an LLM to know about its own documents?
options: It lets the model answer without reading any of the documents at all.
It is the only method that removes the need for an embedding model.
The facts are handed over at request time, so they stay current and can be cited.
It retrains the model on each new document, so the facts end up stored in its weights.
questions.explanation: RAG gives the model the right passage when it is asked. That is fast, cheap, auditable and easy to keep current. Fine-tuning puts knowledge in the weights, which means retraining on every change. RAG needs an embedding model, and the model does read the retrieved text.

questions.prompt: Which of these happen online, once per query? Select all that apply.
options: Building the augmented prompt
Embedding every document chunk
Searching the vector store for the closest chunks
Embedding the query
questions.explanation: Query embedding, retrieval and augmentation happen per query, then generation. Embedding the chunks is part of indexing, done offline and refreshed when the data changes.

questions.prompt: Why does TF-IDF struggle as a RAG retriever?
options: It can only index documents shorter than one sentence.
It needs a GPU to build its tables, which most vector databases don't provide.
It only matches exact words, so a paraphrase with no shared words scores zero.
It produces one vector per word, not one per passage.
questions.explanation: "Canceling a subscription" and "terminate your plan" share no words, so TF-IDF sees nothing in common. One vector per word is Word2Vec's limit, not TF-IDF's. TF-IDF runs on a laptop and handles documents of any length.

questions.prompt: Why does cosine similarity suit comparing chunks of different lengths?
options: It counts shared words, so longer chunks get a fair share of matches against the query.
It divides by the number of tokens, so short chunks are boosted.
It only compares the first 100 dimensions, which all chunks fill.
It measures the angle between vectors, so magnitude doesn't affect the score.
questions.explanation: Cosine similarity depends only on direction. A long chunk and a short one are judged on meaning, not size. Counting shared words is what TF-IDF-style matching does.

questions.prompt: Documents were embedded with one model version. Queries now use a newer version of the same model. What happens?
options: Retrieval improves, because the newer model understands queries better.
The vector store rejects the query, because the dimensions differ.
Nothing, because every version of one model always shares the same vector space.
Retrieval quality collapses, because the two sets of vectors aren't in the same space.
questions.explanation: Procedure 31.2's key rule: same model, same version, for documents and queries. Otherwise distances mean nothing. The dimensions may match, so there may be no error at all, just bad results.

questions.prompt: What does an approximate nearest neighbour index such as HNSW trade?
options: A little recall for a large speedup, from about O(n) toward O(log n)
Memory for accuracy, by storing every vector twice
A little speed in exchange for perfect recall on every single query, however large the store
Embedding quality for a smaller model download
questions.explanation: HNSW may miss a true nearest neighbour now and then, but searches far faster than a brute-force scan. At thousands of chunks brute force is fine. At millions, approximate search is the norm.

questions.prompt: Listing 31.2 passes normalize_embeddings=True. What does that let the system use in place of cosine similarity?
options: Squared Euclidean distance, which ignores direction and so can rank by length alone
Nothing. Normalising has no effect on similarity search.
A plain dot product, since unit vectors' dot product equals their cosine
TF-IDF weighting, since normalised vectors are sparse
questions.explanation: For unit-length vectors, a·b = cos θ, so a dot product gives the cosine directly and is cheaper. Normalised vectors are still dense. Euclidean distance on unit vectors is tied to cosine too, but it does depend on direction.

questions.prompt: What goes wrong when chunks are too large, such as whole documents?
options: A retrieved chunk lacks the surrounding context needed to make sense when read on its own.
The embedding averages every topic in the document, which dilutes the match for any one question.
The vector store refuses to store vectors for long text.
The answer splits across two chunks, and neither ranks high enough.
questions.explanation: A big chunk's embedding blends everything it covers, and it wastes context space on irrelevant text. Missing context and split answers are the problems of chunks that are too small.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter suggest 10 to 20% overlap between consecutive chunks?
options: So the vector store can tell which chunks came from the same source document later on
So every chunk has the same number of tokens, which embeddings need
So an idea that spans a boundary still appears whole in at least one chunk
So duplicate chunks can be removed before embedding
questions.explanation: Overlap repeats a little text at each boundary, so a sentence or idea cut at the edge is intact in the next chunk. It doesn't equalise length or link chunks to their source.

questions.prompt: chunk_by_sentences in Listing 31.1 runs with max_words=10 and overlap_sentences=1 on four sentences of 4 words each. How many chunks does it return?
questions.explanation: Sentences 1 and 2 make 8 words. Adding sentence 3 would make 12, so chunk [1, 2] is closed and the new chunk starts with sentence 2 (the overlap). [2, 3] reaches 8 and closes when sentence 4 would make 12. [3, 4] is left at the end. Three chunks.

questions.prompt: Procedure 31.1 splits on sentence ends instead of a fixed number of characters. What problem does that avoid?
options: A sentence cut mid-thought, which leaves one half meaningless and the other missing context
Sentences that end in a question mark being dropped
Chunks that come out too short to embed with MiniLM
Chunks that the vector store can't give stable IDs to
questions.explanation: The common mistake is character-count chunking that splits sentences. Each half then embeds badly. The regex in the listing splits after ., ! or ?, so questions are kept.

questions.prompt: Why does a RAG system need a similarity threshold and a "no relevant context" path?
options: Vector stores return an error when no chunk passes 0.5 similarity.
The LLM refuses to answer without at least three chunks.
Embedding models return empty vectors for any questions they don't fully understand.
Cosine search always returns something, even when nothing in the store is relevant.
questions.explanation: Similarity search ranks whatever is there. Without a threshold, the model gets irrelevant text and may answer confidently from it. Listing 31.4 drops chunks below min_similarity and switches to a fallback prompt if none are left.

questions.prompt: What does "lost in the middle" mean for how retrieved chunks are ordered in the prompt?
options: Put only one chunk in the prompt, since models read the middle of a long text twice over.
Put the most relevant chunks in the middle, where attention is strongest.
Order chunks at random, since position has no effect.
Put the most relevant chunks at the start or end, since models attend less to the middle.
questions.explanation: Models pay less attention to information in the middle of a long context than at the start or end. So the best chunks shouldn't be buried in the middle.

questions.prompt: build_prompt in Listing 31.4 gets three chunks with scores 0.21, 0.28 and 0.25, and min_similarity=0.3. What prompt does it return?
options: A context prompt with all three chunks, since some context is always better than none
An empty string, which makes the caller skip the LLM call
A context prompt with only the 0.28 chunk, the best of the three
The fallback prompt, which says no relevant context was found
questions.explanation: All three scores are below 0.3, so relevant is empty and the function returns the fallback text. It never keeps a chunk under the threshold, even the best one.

questions.prompt: When does the chapter say fine-tuning beats RAG?
options: When answers need citations to their sources
When the knowledge changes every day
When the goal is to change behaviour or style, not to supply facts
When the document set is far too large to fit inside the model's weights
questions.explanation: RAG can hand a model a fact but can't teach it a new skill. Frequent change, citations and large corpora are all reasons to pick RAG. Many systems use both: fine-tuning for behaviour, RAG for facts.

questions.prompt: What is reranking?
options: Asking the LLM to rank several of its own draft answers and returning the best-scoring one
Sorting retrieved chunks by length before building the prompt
Fetching many candidates cheaply, then re-scoring them with a slower, more accurate model
Re-embedding all documents with a bigger model each night
questions.explanation: Reranking is the chapter's standard fix for the trade-off between retrieving more chunks (better odds) and fewer (less cost and less "lost in the middle" risk). A cheap first pass casts a wide net, and an accurate second pass picks the true top-k.

questions.prompt: A colleague says a model with a million-token context window makes RAG unnecessary. What does the chapter say?
options: Long context eases chunking, but retrieval still scales past any window and costs far less per query.
Correct. With a large enough context window, retrieval adds nothing but latency and cost.
Long context makes RAG worse, because retrieved chunks confuse it.
Correct, as long as the documents fit in the window today.
questions.explanation: The chapter calls this a common confusion. Longer windows reduce the need for aggressive chunking, but a store can outgrow any window, and stuffing megabytes into every prompt costs far more per query.

questions.prompt: A firm's policy documents change weekly, answers must cite the source, and replies must follow a strict house tone. What design fits the chapter's advice?
options: A long-context model with every policy pasted into each prompt
RAG for the changing, citable facts, with fine-tuning only if prompting can't hold the house tone
RAG alone, since retrieving examples of the house tone also teaches the model a new writing style
Fine-tuning alone, retrained weekly so the policies live in the weights
questions.explanation: Weekly change and citations point to RAG for facts. Tone is behaviour, which RAG can't teach, so fine-tuning is the tool if prompting falls short. Weekly retraining is the slow path the chapter warns against, and pasting everything into every prompt is costly.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, what did TF-IDF return for "How do I cancel my subscription?"
options: The correct termination document, but with a low score that barely beat the other five
A similarity of exactly 0 for all six documents, so every candidate tied
The password-reset document, ranked first by mistake
The pricing document, because it mentions subscriptions
questions.explanation: The query shares no words with any document, so TF-IDF scored all six at 0.0000. It didn't retrieve the wrong document. It retrieved nothing. The embedding model ranked the termination document first at 0.5147.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter treat TF-IDF's flat 0.0000 as a useful debugging signal?
options: It shows the LLM ignored the context it was given and answered from memory instead.
It is a visible symptom of a retrieval failure, worth checking before blaming the generation step.
It proves TF-IDF is broken and should never be used.
It means the documents were never indexed.
questions.explanation: The mental model splits RAG failures into retrieval (wrong or no evidence) and generation (right evidence used badly). Every score tied at zero points squarely at retrieval. The documents were indexed. They just share no vocabulary with the query.

questions.prompt: The embedding model scored the right document 0.5147 and the next 0.3638. With Listing 31.4's min_similarity of 0.3, both pass. What risk does that leave, and what fits the chapter?
options: The right document is dropped, because only one chunk can pass.
The password-reset chunk also enters the prompt. Order the best chunk first, or tune the threshold or add a reranker.
The prompt falls back to general knowledge, because two passing chunks conflict with each other and cancel out.
None. Any chunk above the threshold is relevant by definition.
questions.explanation: 0.3638 passes 0.3, so an off-topic chunk joins the context, and irrelevant chunks can pull generation off course. The chapter's tools are ordering (avoid burying the best chunk), threshold choice, and reranking. The function keeps every chunk that passes, and it only falls back when none do.

bookExercises.prompt: List RAG's four online-stage steps in order (embed query, retrieve, augment, generate) and state which two stages happen only once, offline, during indexing.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Online steps, in order: (1) embed the user's query, (2) retrieve the closest chunks from the vector store, (3) augment: build a prompt from the retrieved chunks plus the query, (4) generate: send the augmented prompt to an LLM. Chunking and embedding the document store happen only once, offline, during indexing.

bookExercises.prompt: State the "key rule" from Procedure 31.2 about embedding models, and explain in one sentence what breaks if it's violated.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Always embed queries and documents with the exact same model, pinned to the same version. If violated, e.g. a document store embedded with one model version but queries embedded with a newer version, the two sets of vectors no longer live in a comparable space, and similarity scores become meaningless even though the code runs without error.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 31.5's measured results (embedding top score 0.5147 vs. TF-IDF's 0.0000 across all six documents), explain why TF-IDF's failure here is worse than simply ranking the correct document lower. What specifically does "0.0000 for every document" mean for a system that has to pick a top-k automatically?
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Ranking the correct document lower (say, second or third) still leaves useful signal. A system could return the top-3 and the answer would likely be present. "0.0000 for every document" means there is no signal at all. Every document is exactly tied, so whichever one gets selected as "top-1" is an artifact of sort-stability or array order, not of any actual relevance judgment. A system built on this retrieval would confidently hand the LLM an arbitrary, equally-irrelevant-looking document and prompt it to answer from that. The failure is silent and looks identical to a successful retrieval from the outside.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Procedure 31.4's `build_prompt` function and this chapter's measured TF-IDF results, trace through what `build_prompt` would do if it had been fed TF-IDF's similarity scores for this query with `min_similarity=0.3`, and explain why this is actually the *safer* failure mode compared to what a naive prompt-building function without the threshold check would do.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: With `min_similarity=0.3` and TF-IDF's measured scores all at 0.0000, every candidate falls below the threshold, so `build_prompt` would return the "no relevant context found" fallback path, telling the LLM to answer from general knowledge and say so, rather than handing it an irrelevant document dressed up as ground truth. This is the safer failure mode. A naive prompt builder without the threshold check would take whatever TF-IDF ranked "first" (an arbitrary tie-broken choice) and present it to the LLM as retrieved context, risking a confidently wrong answer grounded in unrelated text: worse than an honest "I don't have relevant context for this."

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague says "we don't need RAG, we'll just fine-tune the model on our documentation every week." Using this chapter's Trade-offs section, write the two or three sentences you'd say about what that plan gets wrong.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "Weekly fine-tuning solves staleness at a real infrastructure and cost burden. Every retrain needs a training run, evaluation, and redeployment, for information that might only have changed in a handful of documents. It also doesn't give auditability. A fine-tuned model can't show which specific document a fact came from, while RAG can cite the exact retrieved passage. And fine-tuning is genuinely good at changing behavior or style, not at being a fact database. Updating documentation weekly via fine-tuning is solving a retrieval problem with a much more expensive and less transparent tool."

bookExercises.prompt: Procedure 31.1's `chunk_by_sentences` uses `overlap_sentences=1` by default. Describe a concrete scenario, using this chapter's Chunking Strategy discussion, where an idea spanning a chunk boundary would still be missed even with this overlap, and what parameter you'd change to fix it.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: If a genuinely complete idea spans three sentences and only the first and last are captured by neighboring chunks (with `overlap_sentences=1` carrying only the single boundary sentence forward), the middle content could still end up split awkwardly if the max_words cutoff falls inside that three-sentence span. Increasing `overlap_sentences` to 2 or 3 would carry more of the preceding context forward into the next chunk, though at the cost of more redundant embedded content and higher storage/embedding cost.

bookExercises.prompt: Read about HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs). Explain in your own words what "approximate" costs in an approximate nearest neighbour search, and why that cost is usually an acceptable trade at the "millions of chunks" scale this chapter describes.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "Approximate" in ANN search means the search is not guaranteed to return the exact true k-nearest-neighbours. It can occasionally miss a genuinely close vector or include one that's slightly further than the true top-k, in exchange for turning what would be an O(n) exhaustive scan into something close to O(log n). At millions-of-chunks scale, this trade is usually acceptable, because RAG retrieval already tolerates some imprecision by design. Reranking (Procedure mentioned in Trade-offs) and threshold filtering are already built to catch and correct for a retrieval step that isn't perfectly precise, so ANN's small accuracy cost rarely changes the end-to-end answer quality, while the latency win is often the difference between a usable and unusable production system.
